items.title: Article 368 — The Amendment Procedure
items.body:
### Amending the Constitution

**In one line**
An amendment is a formal, written change to the Constitution, and **Article 368** is the rule-book that says who can make such a change and how.

**Why it is asked**
The exam loves to test the small procedural details — where a bill starts, what majority is needed, and whether the President can say no. One or two prelims questions almost every year come from here.

**The story**
The makers of the Constitution did not want it to be frozen forever, nor changed on a whim. So they placed the power to amend in **Parliament** (not with the states, not with the people through a referendum) and wrote the steps in **Article 368**, which sits in **Part XX**. The idea of this graded procedure was borrowed from the **South African Constitution**.

Step by step: an amendment bill may be introduced in **either House** of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) — never in a State Legislature — and needs **no prior permission of the President**. Each House must pass it on its own by the required majority; there is **no joint sitting** if the two Houses disagree. Earlier the President could sit on the bill, but the **24th Amendment (1971)** made assent **compulsory** — today the President must sign and cannot withhold or return it.

How big a majority is needed depends on what is being changed. There are three routes, from easiest to hardest.

**Picture it**

| Route | Majority needed | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| Simple majority (outside Article 368) | More than half of the members present and voting | New states, citizenship, quorum, salaries |
| Special majority | More than half of the **total** membership of a House **and** two-thirds of those **present and voting** | Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles |
| Special majority + state approval | The above **plus** approval by at least half the State Legislatures | Federal matters — President's election, Seventh Schedule, Centre-state powers |

Only the last two are counted as amendments **under Article 368**. Simple-majority changes are technically ordinary laws, not constitutional amendments.

**Terms explained**
- **Ratification** — formal approval. Here it means at least half of the State Assemblies must separately pass the bill before a federal change takes effect.
- **Special majority** — two conditions at once: over 50% of the whole House, and two-thirds of only those voting that day.
- **Quorum** — the minimum number of members who must be present for the House to do business.

**Don't confuse**
- Introduced only in **Parliament**, never in a State Legislature (a common trap).
- State approval is needed from **half** the states, **not all** of them.
- The President's assent is **mandatory** (since 1971), unlike an ordinary bill which the President may return once.

**Remember it**
Three majorities, in order of difficulty: **Simple → Special → Special-plus-States** (S-S-S).

**TL;DR**
- Article 368 (Part XX) governs amendments; the procedure idea came from South Africa.
- A bill starts only in Parliament, in either House; no joint sitting.
- 24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent compulsory.
- Three routes: simple majority, special majority, special majority plus approval by half the states.
keyPoints: Article 368 (Part XX) governs amendments; procedure idea borrowed from South Africa.
An amendment bill can be introduced only in Parliament, in either House, not in State Legislatures.
24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent to an amendment bill mandatory.
Special majority = over 50% of total membership of a House + two-thirds of members present and voting.
Federal provisions additionally need approval by at least half the State Legislatures.
Simple-majority changes (new states, citizenship) fall outside the scope of Article 368.

items.title: Landmark Constitutional Amendments
items.body:
### The amendments the exam keeps asking

**In one line**
A handful of amendments changed the Constitution so deeply that their numbers and years are standard exam facts.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-following and 'which amendment did X' questions are almost guaranteed. Knowing the number, the year and the one-line change is enough to score.

**The story**
Since 1951 the Constitution has been amended **106** times (as of 2026). Most were routine, but a few reshaped the document. The very **first** amendment (1951) created the **Ninth Schedule** to shield land-reform laws from court challenge. The **42nd (1976)**, passed during the Emergency, made so many changes that it is nicknamed the **'Mini-Constitution'**. The **44th (1978)** undid several Emergency-era excesses. Later amendments brought in local government (73rd and 74th), the GST (101st), and reservations (103rd, 105th, 106th). The **106th (2023)**, the Women's Reservation Act, is the **latest** amendment as of 2026.

**Picture it**

| Amendment | Year | Key change |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1951 | Added Ninth Schedule; Articles 31A and 31B (land reform) |
| 7th | 1956 | Reorganisation of states — 14 states, 6 Union Territories |
| 42nd ('Mini-Constitution') | 1976 | Socialist, Secular, Integrity in Preamble; Fundamental Duties (Part IVA); All-India Judicial Service |
| 44th | 1978 | Right to property made a legal right (Article 300A); shields Articles 20 and 21 in emergency |
| 52nd | 1985 | Anti-defection law, Tenth Schedule |
| 61st | 1989 | Voting age lowered from 21 to 18 |
| 73rd and 74th | 1992 | Panchayats and urban local bodies (Schedules 11 and 12) |
| 86th | 2002 | Right to Education (Article 21A) |
| 91st | 2003 | Capped Council of Ministers at 15%; tightened anti-defection |
| 101st | 2016 | Goods and Services Tax (GST) |
| 102nd | 2018 | Constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes |
| 103rd | 2019 | 10% reservation for economically weaker sections |
| 105th | 2021 | Restored states' power to identify backward classes |
| 106th | 2023 | Women's Reservation (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) — one-third of seats |

**Terms explained**
- **Ninth Schedule** — a list of laws placed beyond ordinary court challenge; created by the 1st Amendment.
- **Fundamental Duties** — a list of citizens' moral duties, added as Part IVA by the 42nd Amendment.
- **Economically weaker sections (EWS)** — people below an income/asset limit who are not covered by caste-based reservation.

**Don't confuse**
- 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the **42nd (1976)**, not the 44th.
- The **61st** lowered the voting age; the **86th** brought Right to Education — easy to swap.
- 103rd = EWS, 105th = backward-class identification, 106th = women. Keep the trio straight.

**Remember it**
Reservation trio: **103rd = EWS, 105th = backward classes, 106th = Women**.

**TL;DR**
- 1st (1951) added the Ninth Schedule; 42nd (1976) is the 'Mini-Constitution'.
- 44th (1978) made the right to property a legal right under Article 300A.
- 101st (2016) brought GST; 103rd (2019) brought 10% EWS reservation.
- 106th (2023) reserves one-third of seats for women — the latest amendment as of 2026 (106 in total).
keyPoints: 1st Amendment (1951) added the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A/31B.
42nd Amendment (1976), the 'Mini-Constitution', added Socialist/Secular/Integrity and Fundamental Duties.
44th Amendment (1978) made the right to property a legal right under Article 300A.
61st Amendment (1989) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.
73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayats and urban local bodies.
101st (2016) introduced GST; 103rd (2019) gave 10% EWS reservation.
106th Amendment (2023) reserves one-third of seats for women — the latest amendment as of 2026.

items.title: The Basic Structure Doctrine
items.body:
### The Basic Structure Doctrine

**In one line**
Parliament can change the Constitution, but it cannot change the Constitution's core identity — that protected core is called the 'basic structure'.

**Why it is asked**
It is the single most important idea in Indian constitutional law and a favourite of both prelims (which case? which year?) and mains (discuss and evaluate). 

**The story**
Through the 1960s and 1970s a tug-of-war ran between Parliament, which wanted a free hand to amend, and the Supreme Court, which worried that an unlimited power could be used to destroy democracy itself. The clash was settled in **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**. A **13-judge bench** — the largest in Indian history — ruled that Parliament may amend **any** part of the Constitution **but cannot damage or destroy its basic structure**. The judgment date, **24 April 1973**, later became a cut-off date in other cases.

The Court deliberately did **not** give a closed list of what the basic structure contains; judges have filled it in case by case. Features recognised so far include the supremacy of the Constitution, the republican and democratic form of government, the secular character of the state, federalism, separation of powers, **judicial review**, the rule of law, free and fair elections, and the unity and integrity of the nation.

Later cases strengthened the doctrine. **Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** was the **first** case to actually strike down a constitutional provision using the test — a clause of the 39th Amendment that put the Prime Minister's election beyond the courts was void for breaking free and fair elections. **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 and held that limited amending power and judicial review are themselves basic features — 'the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme'. **Waman Rao (1981)** said the test applies to amendments made after 24 April 1973, and **I.R. Coelho (2007)** made post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws open to review.

**Picture it**

| Case | Year | What it did for the doctrine |
|---|---|---|
| Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Created the doctrine (13 judges) |
| Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain | 1975 | First used it to strike a provision |
| Minerva Mills | 1980 | Judicial review is part of it |
| Waman Rao | 1981 | Applies to post-24-April-1973 amendments |
| I.R. Coelho | 2007 | Ninth Schedule laws now reviewable |

**Terms explained**
- **Doctrine** — a principle laid down by courts through judgments, not written in the Constitution.
- **Judicial review** — the power of courts to check whether a law or amendment is constitutional.
- **Basic structure** — the Constitution's unchangeable core identity; open-ended and judge-defined.

**Don't confuse**
- The basic structure is **not defined** in the Constitution — it is judge-made.
- Kesavananda **allowed** amendment of Fundamental Rights (it only barred destroying the core); it did not freeze them.
- The **first** case to apply the doctrine was Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), not Kesavananda itself.

**Remember it**
Kesavananda = '**13 judges, 1973**' — the birth of the basic structure.

**TL;DR**
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973), a 13-judge bench, created the Basic Structure Doctrine.
- Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
- The core is open-ended: supremacy, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, judicial review, rule of law.
- Indira Gandhi (1975) first applied it; Minerva Mills (1980) and I.R. Coelho (2007) reinforced it.
keyPoints: Kesavananda Bharati (1973), a 13-judge bench, propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine.
Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
Elements include supremacy of the Constitution, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, judicial review and rule of law.
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) first applied the doctrine to strike a constitutional provision — the 39th Amendment clause on the PM's election.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Article 368 (4) and (5) and affirmed judicial review as basic.
I.R. Coelho (2007) made post-24-April-1973 Ninth Schedule laws reviewable.
items.mnemonic: Kesavananda = '13 judges, 1973' — the birth of basic structure.

items.title: Amendability of Fundamental Rights — The Case Line
items.body:
### Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights?

**In one line**
The courts changed their mind three times on whether Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights, and the final position is 'yes, but it cannot touch the basic structure'.

**Why it is asked**
The sequence of cases is a classic match-the-following and statement-based theme; getting the order right (1951 → 1967 → 1973) is the whole battle.

**The story**
The question was simple to state but hard to settle: are Fundamental Rights (Part III) beyond Parliament's amending power, or not? In **Shankari Prasad (1951)** the Supreme Court said Parliament **can** amend them, reasoning that a constitutional amendment is not an ordinary 'law' under Article 13(2). **Sajjan Singh (1965)** agreed. Then in **Golaknath (1967)** the Court reversed itself and said Parliament **cannot** amend Part III to take away Fundamental Rights, treating an amendment as 'law'. Parliament hit back with the **24th Amendment (1971)**, declaring it could amend any part. The matter finally settled in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, which **overruled Golaknath**: an amendment is not ordinary 'law', so Fundamental Rights can be amended — but no amendment may destroy the basic structure. Later, **Minerva Mills (1980)** confirmed judicial review as basic, and **I.R. Coelho (2007)** opened post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws to review.

**Picture it**

| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| Shankari Prasad | 1951 | Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights |
| Sajjan Singh | 1965 | Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad |
| Golaknath | 1967 | Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights |
| Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Overruled Golaknath; amendable but not the basic structure |
| Minerva Mills | 1980 | Judicial review is part of the basic structure |
| I.R. Coelho | 2007 | Ninth Schedule laws (post-1973) reviewable |

**Terms explained**
- **Article 13(2)** — bars the state from making 'law' that takes away Fundamental Rights; the whole fight was over whether an amendment counts as such 'law'.
- **Overruled** — a later judgment cancels an earlier one as the governing rule.
- **Part III** — the chapter of the Constitution containing Fundamental Rights.

**Don't confuse**
- Shankari Prasad said 'can'; Golaknath said 'cannot'; Kesavananda said 'can, but not the core'. Order matters.
- The 24th Amendment (1971) came **after** Golaknath and **before** Kesavananda.
- Golaknath did **not** survive — Kesavananda overruled it.

**Remember it**
Amendability tug-of-war: '**Can (1951) → Cannot (1967) → Can, but not the core (1973)**'.

**TL;DR**
- Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): Fundamental Rights are amendable.
- Golaknath (1967): they are not amendable.
- Kesavananda (1973) overruled Golaknath and added the basic-structure limit.
- The 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's response asserting its amending power.
keyPoints: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) upheld Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights.
Golaknath (1967) held Fundamental Rights unamendable, treating an amendment as 'law' under Article 13.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golaknath and introduced the basic-structure limit.
The 24th Amendment (1971) affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part and made assent mandatory.
Parliament's amending power is wide but bounded by the basic structure.
items.mnemonic: Amendability tug-of-war: 'Can (1951) -> Cannot (1967) -> Can, but not the core (1973)'.

items.title: For Mains — Amendments & the Basic Structure
items.body:
## For Mains — how to use this topic in answers

This topic feeds **Paper III (mains-3)**, under the Judiciary / judicial review / amendments clause (syllabus M3-5) and the Constitution clause (M3-1). Mains answers must move beyond 'which amendment did what' to argue how the amending power and the basic-structure doctrine balance **parliamentary sovereignty** against **constitutional supremacy**.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Need / rationale | A living Constitution must adapt; a rigid-only document would break under social change |
| Features | Three-tier procedure (Article 368) blends rigidity and flexibility; graded majorities protect federalism |
| Significance | Basic-structure doctrine preserves constitutional identity against transient majorities |
| Criticism / limits | 'Basic structure' is undefined and open-ended, giving judges wide, unaccountable discretion |
| Way forward | Judicial self-restraint, reasoned use of the doctrine, and respect for the elected legislature's domain |

**Facts, cases and reports to quote**
- **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — 13-judge bench; the doctrine's origin.
- **Minerva Mills (1980)** — judicial review and limited amending power are basic features.
- **I.R. Coelho (2007)** — Ninth Schedule laws post-24 April 1973 are reviewable.
- **NJAC case (99th Amendment, 2015)** — struck down to protect judicial independence, showing the doctrine still bites.
- Over **106 amendments** since 1951 show the document's working flexibility.
- The doctrine has influenced courts in Bangladesh, Pakistan and other Commonwealth states.

**The AP angle**
The AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 and later boundary and local-body changes show how ordinary and special majorities are used in practice; a candidate can cite state reorganisation as an example of flexibility within the federal scheme.

**Use in answers**
- Open with the rigidity-versus-flexibility framing, then anchor each claim to a named case.
- Quote: 'The Constitution is not an end but a means to an end' (reflecting the Kesavananda balance).
- Diagram idea: a simple balance-scale with 'Parliament's amending power' on one pan and 'basic structure' on the other.
keyPoints: Feeds mains-3 (Judiciary / judicial review / amendments, M3-5; Constitution, M3-1).
Frame answers as parliamentary sovereignty vs constitutional supremacy.
Quote Kesavananda (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), I.R. Coelho (2007), NJAC (2015).
Criticism: 'basic structure' is undefined, giving judges wide discretion.
Way forward: judicial restraint and respect for the elected legislature's domain.
